name: Pixwit
tagline: Web app for turning stills and prompts into short AI-generated video clips.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The app itself is a prompt box, an upload field, a job queue and a gallery, all of which an agent can produce in an afternoon. What it is not is the thing doing the work: image-to-video runs on video diffusion models that you either rent per second from fal, Replicate or a model vendor, or run locally on a GPU you probably do not have. So a personal replacement is real and genuinely useful, but it is a shell around someone else's weights, and your output quality is whatever checkpoint you pointed it at. If a tool like this is mostly reselling credits with a nicer interface, the DIY version can be cheaper per clip; if it has done real work on prompt rewriting, shot chaining and preset tuning, you will feel the gap in your first ten renders.
coreLoopDIY: Upload an image, write a motion prompt, fire it at a hosted video model, poll the job, and keep every result in a local gallery with its exact settings.
requirements: An API key for a hosted video model provider (fal.ai, Replicate or similar)
A credit card, since every render costs money per second of output
Node 20 and local disk for storing generated MP4s
Optional: an NVIDIA GPU with 16GB+ VRAM if you want to run open video models locally instead
whatYouLose: Curated model and preset choices, so you do the trial and error on your own dime
Prompt rewriting and safety-net defaults that quietly make mediocre prompts look better
Fast CDN delivery and shareable links; your clips sit on your laptop
Any mobile experience, plus upscaling, frame interpolation and audio if the paid tool bundles them
Someone else absorbing failed renders, queue spikes and model deprecations
moatNotes: The moat is not the UI, it is the relationship with whoever trains and hosts the weights, plus the accumulated knowledge of which settings do not produce melted faces.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because video generation is a cost and taste problem, not a code problem. People pay to skip the part where they burn forty dollars learning that this model needs short prompts and that one needs camera directions, and to get a clip they can post in two minutes without touching an API dashboard. A self-hosted shell gives you full control and a tidy archive, which matters if you render constantly, but it hands you the model selection, the credit management and the failed renders. For a few clips a month, the subscription is cheaper than your own attention.
notes: The interface is a weekend; the weights are not. Build it if you render enough to care about per-clip cost, otherwise just pay.
prompt:
Build a local-only image-to-video studio called "Reel Bench" in an empty folder.

Stack, no substitutions: Next.js 15 with App Router and TypeScript, Tailwind for styling, better-sqlite3 for storage, local filesystem for media. No auth, no accounts, no telemetry, no cloud database. Single user on localhost.

Generation backend: the fal.ai HTTP API via the @fal-ai/client package. Put FAL_KEY in .env.local and read it server-side only. Define the model list in one config file, lib/models.ts, with at least two image-to-video endpoints and one text-to-video endpoint, each with its own parameter schema (duration, aspect ratio, motion strength where supported). Never ship the key to the browser.

Features that are in scope:
- Upload a source image (drag and drop), store it under ./storage/inputs with a hashed filename.
- A composer: source image, prompt textarea, negative prompt, model picker, and the parameters that the selected model actually supports, rendered from the schema.
- Submit creates a job row in SQLite with status queued, then calls fal and stores the request id.
- A server-side poller route that checks in-flight jobs, downloads finished MP4s to ./storage/outputs, and writes status, duration, error text and estimated cost onto the job row.
- A gallery page: grid of generated clips, hover to play muted, click for a detail view showing the full settings used and a "rerun with these settings" button that refills the composer.
- Cost ledger: a simple total of estimated spend this month, computed from a per-model price field in lib/models.ts.
- Delete a job and its files.

Out of scope, do not build: user accounts, sharing links, upscaling, audio, editing or trimming, multi-shot stitching, mobile layouts beyond basic responsive Tailwind.

Requirements: npm install then npm run dev must work with only FAL_KEY set. Handle API failures by writing the error to the job row and showing it in the gallery instead of crashing. Include a README that states plainly that every render costs real money and lists the per-model prices you hardcoded, with a note to verify them against current provider pricing.
